phrases.text: On the evening of 3 October 1964,
people in East Berlin walked to a house on Strelitzer Straße.
Most of them had been told the route
only shortly before they set off.
Their destination was the courtyard behind number 55,
in the district of Mitte.
In the back of that courtyard stood a disused outhouse,
and the passage came up through its floor.
From there it ran about 145 metres under the Berlin Wall to
a bakery on the western side of Bernauer Straße.
Picture a crawlway roughly 80 centimetres wide and 90 centimetres high,
and you have the route. It became known as Tunnel 57,
after the 57 people who came through it
on the nights of 3 and 4 October.
Bernauer Straße was one of the places where
the Wall ran along an ordinary street.
The border ran along the front of the houses,
and those houses stood on East Berlin territory.
After the closures of August 1961, many residents fled at once.
Some let themselves down from their windows, and others jumped into the
rescue sheets that the West Berlin fire brigade held below.
Within a few weeks the houses were cleared,
and their windows and doors were bricked up.
The tunnel of 1964 ran under this same street,
from the West to the East.
The Stiftung's page on the street records that around ten people
died in connection with the border regime here,
all of them in the 1960s.
The street also became a place where people
died trying to get out.
The Stiftung Berliner Mauer names two early deaths here.
Ida Siekmann died on 22 August 1961 after
jumping from a window at Bernauer Straße 48,
and Olga Segler died on 25 September 1961 after
a jump from her window at number 34.
The famous photograph of the border policeman Conrad Schumann leaping over
the wire was taken on this street on 15 August 1961.
The people who crawled through the tunnel
in 1964 were crossing the same border.
The western end of the passage was a rented basement.
Wolfgang Fuchs, a West Berliner who was then 25, rented the rooms
of an empty bakery at number 97 and directed the digging.
He had dug escape tunnels before.
Most of the diggers were students of the Free University of Berlin,
and the youth opposition history page says more than thirty
of them took part. Among them was Reinhard Furrer,
a physics student who later became an astronaut.
On the second night he stood at the gate of the house,
and that is where the trouble began.
The digging ran from April to October 1964.
Counts of the people involved vary.
One account says 35 West Berliners helped to build the tunnel,
and the German Wikipedia article gives the same figure.
The finished passage was 145 metres long and
lay about twelve metres below the surface,
under the Wall rather than along the street.
The youth opposition page gives its height as 90 centimetres and its
width as 80 centimetres, so people had to crawl.
The English Wikipedia article calls it the longest,
deepest and most expensive escape tunnel built in Berlin.
The work cost money.
Part of it came from selling the rights to film and
photograph the tunnel to press and news agencies.
The largest single contribution, about 30,000 Deutschmarks,
came from the West German Federal Ministry for Intra-German Relations,
according to the German Wikipedia article.
The English Wikipedia article adds that the news magazine Stern
helped to finance the project and then reported on
it while keeping its distance from the events.
Money was only one of the problems.
Keeping the plan secret was the other, and a project this
size made that harder with every month of digging.
The tunnel became famous for its length and
for the fact that it worked.
The youth opposition page calls it one of
the most spectacular escapes at the Wall,
and the most successful of roughly seventy tunnel projects of that time.
Its name is the number of people who came through it: 57.
A passage this size, dug over half a year,
was hard to keep secret.
How it stayed hidden for so long was not simple.
It depended on quiet helpers, on a careful list of names,
and on a route that few people knew in full.
The digging broke through to the East on 2 October.
The plan had been to come up in
the cellar of the house on Strelitzer Straße.
Instead, the passage came up in the courtyard,
inside the disused outhouse, a small toilet hut.
People coming through the house therefore had to climb up out of
the earth into a hut in a courtyard, not into a cellar.
The exit was not where the plan had put it.
Even so, the tunnel was ready for the first group,
which walked in on the evening of 3 October.
From the hut, the passage led down and west towards the bakery.
Couriers then informed the would-be escapees,
about 120 people in East Berlin who were to be let out.
Most of them were student friends,
relatives of the students, and their children.
The Chronik der Mauer says the tunnel was meant to help
more than a hundred East Berliners to leave.
The youth opposition page says that the people on the list
learned the route and the entrance only shortly before they went.
The organisers were students of the Free University,
and most of the people they planned to
help were their own friends and relatives.
Secrecy was the core of the plan,
and it was also its weakest point.
Christian Zobel and Hubert Hohlbein received the people at the house,
and Joachim Neumann was the third helper named by the
youth opposition page. Sixty years after the escape,
the Stiftung Berliner Mauer held an event at the Berlin Wall Memorial.
It featured the documentary Heldentod:
Der Tunnel und die Lüge, directed by Britta Wauer,
followed by a conversation with Joachim Neumann and Hubert Hohlbein,
who both took part in the operation.
Their memories make the tunnel more than a list of dates.
The first group walked in during the evening of 3 October,
and the youth opposition page gives the number who
reached West Berlin that first night as 29.
One of them was a child of three and a half.
The first night was the first test of the plan.
Yet the plan had a weak point.
Among the people on the list was an informer for the Stasi,
the East German secret police, who had betrayed the escape plan.
What had he learned about the house at Strelitzer Straße 55
before that first night, and how much had he already reported?
Quick break. I'm Yusuf, and this is Walk of Berlin.
If you enjoy stories like this one,
come and walk one with me.
My walk, Berlin Then and Now,
goes from the World Clock on Alexanderplatz to Hackescher Markt,
with an archive photo at every stop.
You'll find it at walk of berlin dot com.
The second night began on 4 October.
The people waiting in the East were brought to the house in
groups, as they had been the night before.
The youth opposition page says the escapees came
through at intervals of about ten minutes.
Each group was received by helpers such as Zobel,
Hohlbein and Neumann, and led through the courtyard,
the outhouse and the passage. Each group had been
told the route only shortly before it went in.
The Chronik der Mauer describes the night as the continuation of
the same operation, carried on on 4 October.
The count of 57 covers a mixed group.
The youth opposition page breaks the total down this way: 20 men,
27 women, five young people up to the age of 18,
and five children up to the age of 14.
The Chronik der Mauer says the tunnel was
meant to help more than a hundred people,
so not everyone on the list got through.
The tunnel's name counts the people who did get out,
not the longer list of those who had been planned to go.
The Stiftung's event page uses the same total:
57 people escaped on 3 and 4 October.
Meanwhile, the Stasi was searching for the tunnel.
According to the youth opposition page,
officers in plain clothes were searching feverishly for the entrance.
The Chronik der Mauer says the tunnel was
betrayed on the second night.
The Berlin Wall Map says the operation was discovered that night,
when an East German border guard was fatally shot,
and that the escapes ended there. That is when the night turned.
The rest of it played out at the
gate of number 55 and in its courtyard.
The search for the entrance was the first
sign of how the night would go.
Shortly before midnight on 4 October, two Stasi men in plain
clothes came to the gate of the house.
According to the German Wikipedia article,
they gave themselves out as refugees who wanted to go back
and fetch a friend who should come too.
Reinhard Furrer received them at the gate.
According to the youth opposition page, he took them for would-be escapees.
The two men went away again.
The Chronik der Mauer says a Stasi officer then asked for border
troops to help check and arrest suspicious people at the house,
and around half past midnight the men returned with border guards.
The soldiers came back to Strelitzer Straße 55 carrying submachine guns,
according to the youth opposition page.
The Chronik der Mauer says they had been
told to check and arrest suspicious people,
but not the real purpose of the operation.
The escape route was a secret from them.
Among the men who came to the house that night was
Egon Schultz, a sergeant of the border troops.
He was 21 years old. He and the other soldiers had
been called to check people at a house,
and that was all they had been told about why.
According to the youth opposition page,
Christian Zobel first fired a warning shot.
Later he fired more shots to get past the guards,
and one of them hit a border soldier.
Reinhard Furrer ran to the tunnel entrance,
which drew the guards into the courtyard.
The helpers tried to get back towards the passage,
and the night turned violent.
According to the Berlin Wall Map, a guard stumbled upon the exit.
The sources do not agree on every detail of that night,
so this episode keeps to the points on which they are clear.
By the time the Stasi found the entrance,
the youth opposition page says,
28 people had already escaped on the second night.
Added to the 29 of the first night,
that makes 57, the number in the tunnel's name.
The Stiftung Berliner Mauer's event page and the Chronik der
Mauer give the same total of 57 people
for the nights of 3 and 4 October.
The Stiftung's event page does not break the total down by night.
The count of people who got out is clear in the sources,
even though the second-night figure comes from one page alone.
Picture the courtyard at that moment.
The gate to the street is on one side,
the house on another, and the outhouse stands at the back,
where the passage comes up. The passage runs west for
145 metres under the Wall to the bakery.
By then the 28 people of the second night were already across.
The sources do not say how many people were still inside
the house or waiting on the East side when the guards
came through the gate, so that part of the
night cannot be filled in from the record.
What the sources do agree on is the outcome:
the escapes through the tunnel ended that night.
Egon Schultz was born on 4 January 1943 in Pomerania.
He trained as a teacher at the institute in Putbus, and according
to the English Wikipedia article he taught in Rostock-Dierkow before his call-up.
He was conscripted into the National People's Army in 1963,
and the border troops assigned him that November,
according to the Chronik der Mauer.
By August 1964 he had become a candidate for the Communist Party.
He led a group in Border Regiment 34 in Berlin-Mitte,
and he was 21 years old.
The German sources call his rank Unteroffizier,
which this episode renders as sergeant.
On the night of 4 October 1964,
Schultz was a reserve at the command post at Arkonaplatz.
He had not been part of the tunnel operation.
He was sent to the house to check suspicious people,
and he had not been told the real purpose of the operation,
and neither had the soldiers with him.
The Chronik der Mauer records that Christian Zobel fired during that night,
and that one of Zobel's shots hit Schultz in the courtyard.
Sources differ on where Schultz was hit,
so this episode does not say.
The sources do not say what he could see
from where he stood when the shots began.
The fatal shot, according to the Chronik der Mauer,
did not come from an escape helper.
It came from the Kalashnikov of a border soldier who,
on a Stasi officer's instruction,
fired into the dark courtyard and hit Schultz by mistake.
Schultz was taken to the People's Police Hospital and
died on the way there, of internal bleeding.
A 1964 East Berlin investigation, cited there,
found that the fatal shot came from a comrade's Kalashnikov.
The commission report that set this out was found only in 2000,
according to the youth opposition page.
How would the state explain the death of one
of its own soldiers, and who would it blame?
Yusuf again, one more thing before the story goes on.
If you can't join me in person,
my audio walks take you along the Berlin Wall at
Bernauer Straße and through the medieval old town,
at your own pace, on your phone.
They're at walk of berlin dot com.
After the death, the East German press reported that
West Berlin terrorists had murdered a border guard.
The state turned the death into a story about
enemies on the other side of the Wall.
The GDR did not hand over the investigation documents that West Berlin
asked for, so West Berlin dropped its own inquiry,
according to the youth opposition page.
In the official version Schultz became a martyr, and the Chronik der
Mauer calls him a heroic martyr in that account.
The Stiftung Berliner Mauer says the GDR used his death for propaganda.
The GDR gave his name to places that
young people saw every day.
The youth opposition page says that schools,
streets and barracks were named after him,
and that the GDR made him a socialist hero.
The Chronik der Mauer records that more than
a hundred collectives were later named after him,
and that a school in Rostock carried his name.
In August 1966 the southern stretch of Strelitzer Straße was renamed Egon-Schultz-Straße.
The German Wikipedia article gives 12 August and the Chronik gives
13 August, so the exact day is uncertain,
but the month and year agree.
A first plaque at the house was unveiled on 4 January 1965,
the day that would have been Schultz's 22nd birthday.
The Chronik der Mauer says it denounced the
West Berlin agents held responsible for his death.
The English Wikipedia article says that plaque disappeared after 1989.
In 2004, on the fortieth anniversary of his death,
a new plaque was put up at the house by former escape
helpers and a friend of Schultz, according to the English Wikipedia article.
The Chronik der Mauer records that the new plaque
honours him as a victim of the Wall.
The two plaques tell the same death in two very different ways.
The legal aftermath went on for decades.
West Berlin investigated the helpers, and in November 1965 the case ended
with a fine for illegal possession of a weapon,
according to the Chronik der Mauer.
In 1992 a case for suspected negligent homicide was opened,
and the English Wikipedia article says the court accepted that the soldier
who fired the fatal shot had acted in self-defence and had
been ordered to fire, so the case was dismissed.
In May 1994 private individuals pressed charges against Reinhard Furrer, and in
the summer of 1999 the charges against the other helpers were dropped.
Christian Zobel died in the 1980s, and according to the German Wikipedia
article he believed until his death that he had shot the soldier.
The builders went different ways afterwards.
Reinhard Furrer continued his physics studies and became a science astronaut,
according to the German Wikipedia article.
Wolfgang Fuchs and Hasso Herschel, another escape helper of those years,
continued to help people leave the GDR,
according to the English Wikipedia article.
Some of the helpers have since spoken about the tunnel in public,
as Joachim Neumann and Hubert Hohlbein did at the Berlin Wall Memorial.
The people who came through the tunnel were
free in West Berlin that night.
The plaque on the house at number 55 honours Egon Schultz.
The story has been told many times since.
In 2013 the comic book Tunnel 57 by Thomas Henseler and
Susanne Buddenberg was published in Berlin by Ch.
Links Verlag. It runs to 32 pages.
The Stiftung Berliner Mauer's publication page says it draws on authentic
interviews with tunnel builders and refugees, and on original photographs and documents.
Its subject is the 1964 tunnel,
from the West Berlin preparations through the escape to its consequences.
It is a good companion if you want
the story in more detail.
Start at Bernauer Straße 97, on the western side of the street,
where the tunnel began in the basement of the bakery.
A memorial plaque marks the western entrance,
according to the Berlin Wall Map.
Nearby, in the grass of the memorial grounds,
a metal plate in the ground reads Fluchttunnel, Tunnel 57, 1964.
Find it, and then look towards the East,
the direction the passage ran.
The stretch of street where the tunnel ran
was part of the border in 1989 too:
the first wall segments between Bernauer Straße and Eberswalder Straße were broken
open on the night of 10 and 11 November.
The Stiftung's office is at number 111,
and its visitor centre is at number 119.
Then walk to Strelitzer Straße 55,
on the eastern side of the old border, in Berlin-Mitte.
The street regained its old name, Strelitzer Straße, on 1 December 1991,
after the fall of the Wall and the
Berlin Senate's new responsibility for the whole city.
The tunnel ended in the courtyard of this house.
The plaque on the house honours Egon Schultz
as a victim of the Wall,
and according to the English Wikipedia article it also marks the escape.
Stand for a minute in front of it.
Read what it says, and think of the young soldier who died
in the courtyard behind that house, and of the 57 people
who came through the tunnel in those two nights.
That's this week's story.
I'm Yusuf, and if you want to stand where it happened,
my walks and audio walks are at walk of berlin dot com.
